name: Lena Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I build and repair power lines for the electricity company, usually with one other lineworker in the truck. My vocational certificate and apprenticeship taught me the hands-on part; these days I use AI every day to sort fault notes before I write the handover. I like tracing why a street went dark, then checking the repair against a real meter. My partner Ravi and I have grown children, more than six months of expenses saved, and higher pay for this job. I can see retirement ahead, but I have not chosen a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot I can live with modest software if it clears the office backlog. I still want the original meter readings attached to every AI summary of a line repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI already helps me write notes, so a plateau would not make my job feel smaller. Our savings and pay give us room to plan retirement at our own pace, and I would keep checking the tool for confident mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue repair shifts and compare each generated handover with the meter sheet before sending it. In the first year I would show the newest worker how to flag a missing reading in the AI summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A slow AI report tool is still useful if I can see exactly where it got the facts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What missing reading would you demonstrate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a report that names the replaced connector but leaves out the voltage test afterward. The apprentice would mark the blank before the next crew leaves the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Ravi and I would check our finances in the usual way; a small software change is not a reason to stop working.

say: **AI summaries** may clear office backlog if original meter readings remain attached.
**Hands-on repair** still relies on a lineworker checking the physical result.
think: I already use **AI daily**, so a plateau leaves my work largely secure.
Our **higher pay and savings** allow retirement planning without a rush.
do: **Continue** line repair shifts and verify AI handovers against meter sheets.
**Show** a new worker how to flag a missing reading in an AI summary.
feel: **Calm** about work and money, alert to factual errors.
S0.quote: A slow AI report tool is still useful if I can see exactly where it got the facts.
fieldNote: She uses **AI daily** in a narrow, practical way for fault notes.
Her **savings and high pay** make ordinary retirement timing a choice rather than an immediate need.

steps.text: Continue line repair shifts while checking AI handovers
Teach new worker to flag missing readings in AI summaries

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say dispatch will change before the line truck does, and I would rather test its new fault map than complain at a lunch table. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might get better fault locations, but the office may remove a second checker and send incomplete jobs to us. I do not expect a cut in my own pay yet; other utilities nearby need experienced workers, and our savings cover a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the new map on eight fault calls, recording where the location or access is wrong. During the first year I would show those cases to the dispatch supervisor and keep using the map only for the calls it handles accurately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the office colleagues and the crew’s safety, but fairly secure at home. I would rather measure what works than guess about the fault map from a depot lunch table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which call would expose a bad map?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A feeder fault beside a school can have two access gates, and the map may send our truck to the locked one. I would record the lost time and the correct gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the union to step in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If dispatch staffing is cut and the missing checks reach the crew, I would bring the record to our union representative. A test alone would not tell me how the staffing decision is being made.

say: **Dispatch AI** reaches fault locations before field robots change repairs.
**Eight-call trial** can show whether the map handles real access.
think: Losing an **office checker** could send incomplete work orders to the crew.
My **own pay** appears secure for now given savings and nearby utilities.
do: **Test** the fault map on eight calls and log wrong access gates.
**Show** errors to dispatch and restrict use to accurate calls.
feel: **Uneasy** about safety and office colleagues, financially secure at home.
S1.quote: I would rather measure what works than guess about the fault map from a depot lunch table.
fieldNote: She favours a **field trial** before accepting or rejecting the map.
A **union approach** remains conditional on staffing cuts, so it is not tagged as an action now.

steps.text: Test AI fault map on eight calls and log wrong access gates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 changes dispatch, while robots that can repair lines as well as people follow around 2031. I want to learn the robot controls before one arrives beside our truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty or so when thinking AI appears, I could still want several years of field pay. If robots take part of our repair rota by 2031, I could lose that pay even with strong savings and plenty of local utilities; they might all be testing the same machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a place in a company robot-controls trial and learn the controls on dead equipment before anyone uses them near a live line. In the first year after 2028 I would apply for a paid field verification post if one opens locally at a wage that covers our bills; if none does, I would keep repair shifts and ask nearby utilities about actual vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can still act. I do not want my last working years decided by a demo that never touched an old pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise stopping the robot when its isolation reading and the meter disagree. I want my hand to know where the robot stop control is before any live-line trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ravi about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Ravi we can cover a short gap from savings, but should compare any new wage with our regular bills. We would not set a retirement date from the first trial result.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches dispatch before field robots arrive around 2031.
**Robot controls** should be learned on dead equipment before live-line use.
think: Repair robots could cut my **late-career pay** after 2031.
Savings and **local utilities** help, but may not replace the same wage.
do: **Learn** robot stop controls in a company trial on dead equipment.
**Apply** after 2028 for local paid verification if a bill-covering vacancy opens.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to practise and search.
S2.quote: I want my hand to know where the robot stop control is before any live-line trial.
fieldNote: She seeks **hands-on robot controls** early, consistent with daily AI use and risk tolerance.
Her **job application** depends on an actual local post and wages sufficient for household bills.

steps.text: Learn robot stop controls on dead equipment in company trial
Apply for local paid field verification after 2028 if bill-covering vacancy opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me test a robot in more than one weather season before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Field robots come about 2034, and I would like the crew to write the stop checklist, not inherit one unseen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be around sixty-three at the first date and around sixty-six at the second. Retirement might suit us by then, but I want a real household calculation before treating the robot date as the end of my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking repair shifts and review income and expenses with Ravi every year. I would join the crew safety committee to draft a robot stop checklist before 2031; in the first year after 2031 I would stay in field work if safe hours remain and the retirement numbers are not ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful, with more room than in the fast picture. A checklist I helped test would matter more than a promise that a repair robot is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the checklist ask first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should ask whether the machine’s isolation reading matches the crew’s own meter. If the readings disagree, the crew stops the work before a robot touches the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if retirement is affordable by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi and I might choose to stop then, but we would decide from our own costs and wishes. I would not call the robot schedule a retirement instruction.

say: **Seasonal robot tests** give crews evidence before field machines arrive around 2034.
**Crew stop rules** should be written by workers who test the equipment.
think: Retirement by **2034** is possible but unconfirmed.
The **household calculation** matters more than a machine launch date for my work and retirement.
do: **Review** income and retirement costs with Ravi each year while repairing lines.
**Join** crew safety committee to draft a robot stop checklist.
feel: **Watchful**, with time to shape safer field rules.
S3.quote: A checklist I helped test would matter more than a promise that a repair robot is safe.
fieldNote: She reserves a **retirement decision** for actual household figures, without promising an earlier date.
Her **committee work** is an explicit group activity to set field robot stop rules.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and review retirement costs with Ravi yearly
Join crew safety committee to draft robot stop checklist

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade puts thinking AI in 2036 and full field robots around 2039. I would use the years to leave good fault records for younger workers, then decide when to stop by what Ravi and I can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives, so I may be retired by then. If I am still doing line repairs, I could work with a machine on a smaller rota, but I would not assume a new paid role is waiting for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current repair shifts for now and check the retirement budget with Ravi each year. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would help the crew test robot handovers against meter readings; if retired, I would leave the field decisions to those on the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own income outlook, while still caring about the records I leave. Ten years is enough for us to plan without guessing a date tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good record include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fault record should show the original meter value, the repair made and the test afterward. The next line crew should be able to reconstruct the power-line condition without asking who wrote the summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a new course at sixty-eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I were still employed and the company offered paid instruction on the machine we actually used. I would not buy a qualification for a job I might never hold.

say: **Fault records** should preserve meter values and repair tests for younger crews.
**2036 thinking AI** arrives before field robots around 2039.
think: I may be **retired** before thinking AI arrives at roughly sixty-eight.
If still working, I cannot assume a **paid robot role** will appear.
do: **Keep** repair shifts and review retirement budget with Ravi yearly.
**Check** robot handovers against meter sheets after 2036 only if still employed.
feel: **Calm** about the long runway, attentive to records left behind.
S4.quote: The next line crew should be able to reconstruct the power-line condition without asking who wrote the summary.
fieldNote: Her **long horizon** may carry her beyond work, without a forced retirement date.
She would check **robot handovers** only if still employed; course interest remains conditional and untagged.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and review retirement budget with Ravi yearly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because field robots around 2031 could shorten my high-pay years before Ravi and I choose a retirement date. A paid local verification opening and time on the robot controls before a live-line trial would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether the person watching a robot will have authority to stop it. I would want the repair robot stop control in a lineworker’s hand, not locked behind an office approval.

portrait: **Lena Petrov**, 58, is an experienced mid-level power lineworker with a vocational certificate and apprenticeship.
She and partner Ravi have **grown children**, higher lineworker pay and more than six months of expenses saved.
She uses **AI daily** for fault notes, checks meter sheets and wants to practise robot stop controls early.
In **Steady Disruption**, she tests a fault map and keeps union action conditional on actual staffing cuts.
The **2028 scenario** concerns her most because robots could trim late-career pay before she chooses retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce her high-pay repair shifts after field robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A paid **local verification job** with bill-covering wages would offer a route if repairs shrink.
Hands-on **robot control practice** before live-line use would give her and the crew safer choices.
headlineQuote: I would want the repair robot stop control in a lineworker’s hand, not locked behind an office approval.
